etymology: Greek Smurna, related to smurna, "myrrh" — the bitter, fragrant resin used for embalming. A fitting name for the church of suffering, whose faithfulness was crushed like myrrh into sweetness before God.
biblical_def: Smyrna was a wealthy port city of the Roman province of Asia, north of Ephesus, and the second of the seven churches addressed by the glorified Christ in the Revelation (Rev 2:8-11). To Smyrna alone, with Philadelphia, the Lord speaks no word of rebuke. He presents Himself as "the first and the last, which was dead, and is alive" — the very comfort a persecuted, dying church needs. He knows their works, their tribulation, and their poverty, and then adds the great reversal: "but thou art rich" (Rev 2:9). They were materially poor and slandered by "them which say they are Jews, and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan." The Lord does not promise escape but forewarns of prison and "tribulation ten days," calling them to a costly fidelity: "be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life" (Rev 2:10). The overcomer "shall not be hurt of the second death." Smyrna is the pattern of the suffering church in every age — poor in this world, rich toward God, and faithful unto the scaffold. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, would in the next century seal this very testimony with his blood.
webster_summary: The persecuted port-city church of Revelation 2:8-11, poor yet rich, slandered by the synagogue of Satan, called to be faithful unto death for the crown of life; one of only two churches the Lord does not rebuke.
webster_full: SMYRNA, proper noun. A wealthy port city of Asia Minor; the second of the seven churches of the Revelation (Rev 2:8-11).
Addressed by Christ as "the first and the last, which was dead, and is alive."
A church of poverty and persecution — yet pronounced rich (Rev 2:9).
Slandered by the synagogue of Satan; forewarned of tribulation ten days.
Called to be faithful unto death for the crown of life; the overcomer escapes the second death.
scriptures: Rev 2:8
And unto the angel of the church in Smyrna write; These things saith the first and the last, which was dead, and is alive;
Rev 2:9
I know thy works, and tribulation, and poverty, (but thou art rich) and I know the blasphemy of them which say they are Jews, and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Rev 2:11
He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death.
corruption_summary: Smyrna is corrupted when its poverty-yet-riches is inverted into a prosperity gospel, or when its call to be faithful unto death is softened into a promise of earthly comfort and escape from suffering.
corruption_paragraphs: Prosperity-gospel inversion. The health-and-wealth teacher reads "but thou art rich" as a pledge of material increase, exactly reversing the Lord's meaning. Smyrna was materially poor and spiritually rich — the riches are treasure in heaven, not gold on earth. The Lord promises this faithful church not prosperity but prison, not ease but a crown won through death. To preach Smyrna as a wealth text is to preach the precise opposite of the words, flattering the flesh where Christ steeled the soul for martyrdom.

Suffering-denied misreading. Modern therapeutic religion recoils from "be thou faithful unto death" and recasts the Christian life as a path to self-actualization and emotional well-being. But the Lord of Smyrna does not spare His people tribulation; He sanctifies them through it and crowns them after it. The dictionary holds with Scripture that the church is often called to suffer, that faithfulness may cost everything, and that the crown of life is laid up for those who love not their lives unto the death (Rev 12:11).
roots_summary: The persecuted myrrh-named church of Revelation 2, poor yet rich, called to faithfulness unto death for the crown of life.

etymology: Greek Pergamos, "citadel, height." A leading city of Asia Minor, center of the imperial cult and of pagan worship — called by the Lord the place "where Satan's seat is."
biblical_def: Pergamos was the political capital of Roman Asia and a stronghold of idolatry, home to the great altar of Zeus and a leading center of emperor worship. It is the third of the seven churches of the Revelation (Rev 2:12-17). The Lord, presenting Himself with "the sharp sword with two edges," commends the church for holding fast His name even "where Satan's seat is" — even in the days of Antipas, "my faithful martyr, who was slain among you" (Rev 2:13). Yet He has a controversy: some hold "the doctrine of Balaam," who taught Balak to seduce Israel into idolatry and fornication, and some hold "the doctrine of the Nicolaitans, which thing I hate" (Rev 2:15). The danger at Pergamos was not open persecution but compromise — the tolerating of false teachers within the assembly. The Lord calls them sharply to repentance: "Repent; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will fight against them with the sword of my mouth" (Rev 2:16). To the overcomer He promises "to eat of the hidden manna," and "a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it" (Rev 2:17). Pergamos is the church that stands firm under pressure but grows lax toward doctrinal corruption from within.
webster_summary: The third church of Revelation (2:12-17), planted "where Satan's seat is," faithful under persecution yet rebuked for tolerating the doctrine of Balaam and the Nicolaitans; promised hidden manna and a white stone with a new name.
webster_full: PERGAMOS, proper noun. The capital of Roman Asia and a center of idolatry and emperor worship.
The third of the seven churches (Rev 2:12-17), called the place "where Satan's seat is."
Commended for holding fast Christ's name even when Antipas was martyred there.
Rebuked for tolerating the doctrine of Balaam and of the Nicolaitans.
Promised hidden manna and a white stone with a new name to the overcomer.
scriptures: Rev 2:12
And to the angel of the church in Pergamos write; These things saith he which hath the sharp sword with two edges;
Rev 2:13

I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you, where Satan dwelleth.
Rev 2:16
Repent; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will fight against them with the sword of my mouth.
Rev 2:17

He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.
corruption_summary: Pergamos is corrupted when doctrinal tolerance is celebrated as a virtue, so that the very Balaamism and Nicolaitanism the Lord hates is reframed as inclusive, generous, and loving.
corruption_paragraphs: Tolerance-as-virtue inversion. The modern church often prizes the toleration of false teaching as broad-mindedness and love. The Lord of Pergamos calls it sin. He hates the doctrine of the Nicolaitans and threatens to come and fight against the compromisers with the sword of His mouth. Doctrinal vigilance is not narrowness; it is faithfulness. The dictionary holds that the church must hold fast Christ's name and refuse the leaven of false teaching — the two are one obedience, not a tension to be balanced.

Balaam-domesticated misreading. The doctrine of Balaam is the strategy of corrupting God's people from within by seducing them into idolatry and immorality when frontal assault fails (Num 25; 31:16). Liberal scholarship often treats Balaam as a quaint folk-villain and empties the warning of force. Scripture treats his doctrine as a live and deadly danger reaching into the New-Covenant church. The dictionary recovers the warning: compromise dressed as openness is Satan's seat established inside the assembly.
roots_summary: The third church of Revelation, faithful under persecution at Satan's seat yet rebuked for tolerating Balaam and the Nicolaitans; promised hidden manna and a white stone.

etymology: Greek Thuateira, a city of Lydia famed for its trade guilds and its dyers of purple — the home town of Lydia, the seller of purple converted at Philippi (Acts 16:14).
biblical_def: Thyatira was a commercial city of Asia Minor known for its trade guilds, and the fourth of the seven churches of the Revelation (Rev 2:18-29). It receives the longest of the seven letters. The Lord presents Himself as "the Son of God, who hath his eyes like unto a flame of fire, and his feet are like fine brass" — the searcher of hearts and the treader of judgment. He commends their charity, service, faith, patience, and growth: "the last to be more than the first" (Rev 2:19). Yet He has a grave charge: "thou sufferest that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols" (Rev 2:20). The sin of Thyatira is the toleration of a false prophetess whose teaching led the people into the idolatry and immorality bound up with the trade guilds. The Lord gave her space to repent; refusing, she and her followers face His judgment, "and all the churches shall know that I am he which searcheth the reins and hearts" (Rev 2:23). To the faithful remnant who have not known "the depths of Satan," He says, "hold fast till I come" (Rev 2:25), and promises power over the nations and "the morning star."
webster_summary: The fourth church of Revelation (2:18-29), commended for growing love and service yet sharply rebuked for tolerating "that woman Jezebel," a false prophetess seducing the servants of God into idolatry and immorality; the faithful remnant is promised the morning star.
webster_full: THYATIRA, proper noun. A commercial city of Lydia famed for trade guilds and purple dye; the fourth of the seven churches (Rev 2:18-29).
Addressed by the Son of God with eyes like a flame of fire and feet like fine brass.
Commended for charity, service, faith, patience, and increasing works.
Rebuked for suffering the false prophetess Jezebel to seduce God's servants.
The faithful remnant called to hold fast; promised rule over the nations and the morning star.
scriptures: Rev 2:18
And unto the angel of the church in Thyatira write; These things saith the Son of God, who hath his eyes like unto a flame of fire, and his feet are like fine brass;
Rev 2:19
I know thy works, and charity, and service, and faith, and thy patience, and thy works; and the last to be more than the first.
Rev 2:20

Notwithstanding I have a few things against thee, because thou sufferest that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols.
Rev 2:25
But that which ye have already hold fast till I come.
corruption_summary: Thyatira is corrupted when the rebuke of Jezebel is recast as intolerance, so that the discernment Christ demands is condemned as judgmental and the false prophetess is defended in the name of inclusion.
corruption_paragraphs: Discernment-as-bigotry inversion. The Lord's complaint against Thyatira is not that it judged Jezebel but that it suffered her — tolerated a self-appointed prophetess whose teaching corrupted the flock. The modern instinct reverses this, treating the church's discernment as the sin and the false teacher's "authenticity" as the virtue. Christ with eyes like flame commends the church for everything except its tolerance of error. The dictionary recovers that love and discernment are not opposites: the church that truly loves its people guards them from the Jezebels who would seduce them.

Jezebel-spiritualized misreading. Some empty this warning by treating "Jezebel" as mere metaphor with no doctrinal teeth, or by recasting the named sins — fornication and idolatry — as culturally relative. Scripture names them as real and damning, and ties them to the trade-guild idolatry that pressured Thyatiran believers to compromise for their livelihood. The dictionary holds that Christ still searches the reins and hearts, still calls false teachers to account, and still rewards the faithful remnant who refuse the depths of Satan.
roots_summary: The fourth church of Revelation, commended for growing service yet rebuked for tolerating the false prophetess Jezebel; the faithful remnant promised the morning star.

etymology: Greek Sardeis, the ancient capital of Lydia, once the seat of Croesus and a byword for wealth. By the Lord's day a city living on its past glory — a fitting emblem of the church with a name to live, yet dead.
biblical_def: Sardis was the old capital of Lydia, twice captured in history because its watchmen slept on its supposedly impregnable acropolis. It is the fifth of the seven churches of the Revelation (Rev 3:1-6). The Lord, "he that hath the seven Spirits of God, and the seven stars," pierces its reputation with one of the most searching verdicts in Scripture: "I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead" (Rev 3:1). Sardis had a reputation for vitality but was spiritually a corpse. The Lord's remedy is urgent: "Be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain, that are ready to die" (Rev 3:2). He warns that if they will not watch, "I will come on thee as a thief, and thou shalt not know what hour I will come upon thee" — the very judgment that twice took the sleeping city. Yet even in Sardis there is grace: "thou hast a few names even in Sardis which have not defiled their garments; and they shall walk with me in white: for they are worthy" (Rev 3:4). To the overcomer the Lord promises white raiment, that his name shall not be blotted out of the book of life, and that Christ will confess his name before the Father and the angels. Sardis is the warning to the church that mistakes reputation for life.
webster_summary: The fifth church of Revelation (3:1-6), with a name that it lived but was dead; called to watch and strengthen what remained, lest Christ come as a thief; a faithful few who had not defiled their garments are promised white raiment and the book of life.
webster_full: SARDIS, proper noun. The old capital of Lydia, a city living on past glory; the fifth of the seven churches (Rev 3:1-6).
Addressed by him that hath the seven Spirits of God and the seven stars.
Indicted with the verdict: a name to live, yet dead.
Called to be watchful and strengthen the things that remain, ready to die.
A faithful few with undefiled garments promised white raiment and the book of life.
scriptures: Rev 3:1

And unto the angel of the church in Sardis write; These things saith he that hath the seven Spirits of God, and the seven stars; I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead.
Rev 3:2
Be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain, that are ready to die: for I have not found thy works perfect before God.
Rev 3:4
Thou hast a few names even in Sardis which have not defiled their garments; and they shall walk with me in white: for they are worthy.
Rev 3:5
He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels.
corruption_summary: Sardis is corrupted when outward reputation, programs, and numbers are mistaken for spiritual life, and when the call to watchfulness is dismissed as alarmism in a church the Lord has already pronounced dead.
corruption_paragraphs: Reputation-for-life inversion. Sardis exposes the deadliest of church diseases: a living name over a dead body. The modern church often measures health by attendance, budgets, buildings, and buzz — the very "name to live" the Lord pierces through. He looks past the reputation to the works He has not found perfect before God. The dictionary holds with Christ that vitality is not reputation; a church may be celebrated by men and reckoned a corpse by its Head, and the only remedy is to wake, watch, and strengthen what remains.

Watchfulness-dismissed misreading. The command "be watchful" cuts against a religion that prefers comfort to vigilance. Sardis fell in history because its guards slept; the Lord uses the city's own shame as His warning. To treat the call to watch as needless alarm is to repeat Sardis's sin. The dictionary recovers the New Testament's sober insistence that the church must watch, for the Lord comes as a thief upon the unready (Rev 3:3; 1 Thess 5:2-6).
roots_summary: The fifth church of Revelation, with a name to live yet dead, called to watch and strengthen what remains; the faithful few promised white raiment and the book of life.

etymology: Greek Philadelpheia, "brotherly love," from philos (loving) and adelphos (brother). A city of Lydia named for the brotherly devotion of its founder — and the church of the open door.
biblical_def: Philadelphia was a city of Lydia on a major trade route, and the sixth of the seven churches of the Revelation (Rev 3:7-13). With Smyrna, it receives no rebuke. The Lord presents Himself as "he that is holy, he that is true, he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth" (Rev 3:7). To this church of "a little strength" that has "kept my word, and hast not denied my name," He gives a magnificent promise: "I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it" (Rev 3:8). Those of "the synagogue of Satan" who slandered them will be made to bow and to know that Christ has loved them. Because they kept "the word of my patience," the Lord promises to keep them "from the hour of temptation, which shall come upon all the world" (Rev 3:10). He exhorts, "hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown" (Rev 3:11). To the overcomer He promises to make him "a pillar in the temple of my God," bearing the name of God, the name of the New Jerusalem, and Christ's own new name (Rev 3:12). Philadelphia is the faithful, weak, persevering church for whom Christ Himself opens doors no power on earth can shut.
webster_summary: The sixth church of Revelation (3:7-13), of little strength yet faithful, set before an open door no man can shut, kept from the hour of temptation, and promised to be made a pillar in the temple of God; one of only two churches the Lord does not rebuke.
webster_full: PHILADELPHIA, proper noun. "Brotherly love"; a city of Lydia and the sixth of the seven churches (Rev 3:7-13).
Addressed by him that is holy and true, who has the key of David.
Commended for keeping Christ's word and not denying His name, though of little strength.
Set before an open door no man can shut; kept from the hour of temptation.
The overcomer made a pillar in God's temple, bearing the name of God and of the New Jerusalem.
scriptures: Rev 3:7

And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write; These things saith he that is holy, he that is true, he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth;
Rev 3:8
I know thy works: behold, I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it: for thou hast a little strength, and hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name.
Rev 3:10
Because thou hast kept the word of my patience, I also will keep thee from the hour of temptation, which shall come upon all the world, to try them that dwell upon the earth.
Rev 3:12

Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name.
corruption_summary: Philadelphia is corrupted when the "open door" is reduced to a slogan for worldly opportunity or church-growth strategy, severed from the holiness, fidelity, and patient endurance the Lord actually commends.
corruption_paragraphs: Open-door-as-opportunism misreading. The promise "I have set before thee an open door" is endlessly borrowed for ventures, ambitions, and programs the text never addresses. In Revelation the open door is Christ's sovereign provision for a faithful, weak church that kept His word and did not deny His name — an opening of gospel access and final entrance into the temple of God. The dictionary holds that Christ alone, who has the key of David, opens and shuts; the door is His gift to fidelity, not a charm for human enterprise.

Kept-from-temptation misapplied. "I will keep thee from the hour of temptation" is variously stretched and shrunk in eschatological debate; whatever one's millennial frame, the dictionary insists on the plain comfort: Christ preserves His faithful people through trial because they kept the word of His patience. The promise rewards perseverance, not presumption. To claim the keeping while neglecting the patient obedience that occasions it is to take the comfort and refuse the cross.
roots_summary: The sixth church of Revelation, weak yet faithful, set before an open door no man can shut and promised to be made a pillar in the temple of God.

etymology: From the seven literal assemblies of Roman Asia named in Revelation 1:11 — Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea — addressed by the glorified Christ through John.
biblical_def: The seven churches are the seven actual first-century congregations of the Roman province of Asia to whom the risen, glorified Christ dictates letters through the apostle John in Revelation 2-3. They are named in order along a circular postal route: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea (Rev 1:11). John sees the Lord walking "in the midst of the seven candlesticks," holding "seven stars" in His right hand; He Himself interprets them: "the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches: and the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches" (Rev 1:20). Each letter follows a pattern: a title of Christ drawn from the vision, a commendation (except to Sardis and Laodicea), a rebuke (except to Smyrna and Philadelphia), a command, and a promise to the overcomer. Because seven is the number of completeness, these real letters to real churches also speak to the whole church through all ages, and each closes with the universal summons, "He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches." The seven churches are at once a snapshot of Asia in John's day and a mirror in which every congregation must examine itself before the eyes of its Lord, who walks among the lampstands and knows their works.
webster_summary: The seven literal congregations of Roman Asia — Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea — addressed by the glorified Christ in Revelation 2-3, each with a commendation, rebuke, command, and promise to the overcomer.
webster_full: SEVEN CHURCHES, noun phrase. The seven congregations of Asia addressed in Revelation 2-3 (named Rev 1:11).
Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea, in postal-route order.
Christ walks among the seven candlesticks and holds the seven stars (Rev 1:20).
Each letter gives a title of Christ, commendation, rebuke, command, and overcomer's promise.
Real letters to real churches, yet a mirror for the whole church in every age.
scriptures: Rev 1:11

Saying, I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last: and, What thou seest, write in a book, and send it unto the seven churches which are in Asia; unto Ephesus, and unto Smyrna, and unto Pergamos, and unto Thyatira, and unto Sardis, and unto Philadelphia, and unto Laodicea.
Rev 1:13
And in the midst of the seven candlesticks one like unto the Son of man, clothed with a garment down to the foot, and girt about the paps with a golden girdle.
Rev 1:20

The mystery of the seven stars which thou sawest in my right hand, and the seven golden candlesticks. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches: and the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches.
Rev 2:7
He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God.
corruption_summary: The seven churches are corrupted when they are dissolved into pure allegory or astrological-style church-age schemes that deny their concrete first-century reality, or when their searching rebukes are softened so no living church need examine itself.
corruption_paragraphs: Allegory-only misreading. Some empty the seven letters of historical substance, treating them as mere symbols with no real congregations behind them; others build elaborate prophetic timetables in which each church secretly stands for a successive "age" of church history. The text resists both. These were real assemblies with named sins, named martyrs (Antipas), and named false teachers; their completeness (seven) extends the application to the whole church without erasing the history. The dictionary holds the letters as literal and exemplary at once — addressed to Asia, binding on all.

Rebuke-softened misreading. A sentimental reading lingers on the commendations and mutes the warnings — the dead works of Sardis, the lukewarmness of Laodicea, the tolerated Jezebel of Thyatira. But Christ walks among the lampstands as Judge as well as Comforter, threatening to remove candlesticks and spue the lukewarm from His mouth. The dictionary recovers the full voice of the letters: every church stands under the searching gaze of its Lord, who calls each to repent and overcome.
roots_summary: The seven literal congregations of Asia addressed by the glorified Christ in Revelation 2-3, each given a commendation, rebuke, command, and promise; a mirror for the whole church.

etymology: From Revelation 17:5, where the title is written upon the forehead of the great harlot: "MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH." Mystery (Greek musterion) marks it as a symbol to be discerned, not the literal Mesopotamian city.
biblical_def: Mystery Babylon is the symbolic name given in the Revelation to the great end-time system of idolatry, seduction, and persecution that opposes God and martyrs His saints. In Revelation 17 John sees "a woman sit upon a scarlet coloured beast," arrayed in purple and scarlet and decked with gold, holding "a golden cup in her hand full of abominations and filthiness of her fornication" (Rev 17:4). Upon her forehead is written the title of mystery: Babylon the Great, the mother of harlots. She is "drunken with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus" (Rev 17:6). The name reaches back to the original Babel, the city of human pride that set itself against heaven (Gen 11), and forward to every God-defying civilization that trades in luxury, idolatry, and the blood of the faithful. Revelation 18 sings her fall: "Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen," and calls God's people out of her: "Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins" (Rev 18:4). Mystery Babylon is thus the whole spirit of the world organized against the Lamb — commercial, religious, and political — destined for sudden and total judgment, that the marriage of the Lamb may come.
webster_summary: The symbolic harlot-city of Revelation 17-18, the great end-time system of idolatry and persecution drunk with the blood of the saints; the heir of Babel and the spirit of the world against God, called "the mother of harlots" and destined for sudden judgment.

corruption_summary: Mystery Babylon is corrupted when it is flattened into a single partisan target for conspiracy-mongering, or when it is emptied of all reference so that the world-system's real idolatry, luxury, and martyr-blood are no longer named and renounced.
corruption_paragraphs: Conspiracy-flattening misreading. Babylon is endlessly pinned on one institution, nation, or party by readers eager to decode the beast on the evening news. Scripture paints a fuller picture: a trans-historical system of idolatry, commerce, and persecution stretching from Babel to the end, the very spirit of the world arrayed against the Lamb. The dictionary holds the symbol with sobriety — Babylon is wherever pride, luxury, false worship, and the blood of the saints converge — and refuses to shrink a cosmic warning into a partisan slogan.

Reference-emptied misreading. The opposite error treats Babylon as a vague literary flourish with no claim on the conscience. But the angel's command is concrete: "Come out of her, my people." The world-system makes real demands and offers real seductions, and the church is summoned to visible separation from its idolatry and its sins. The dictionary recovers both the symbol's breadth and its bite: Babylon is judged, and God's people must not be found sharing her cup.

etymology: From Revelation 2:9 and 3:9, where the glorified Christ names those "which say they are Jews, and are not, but do lie" — a false, persecuting assembly opposed to the true people of God.
biblical_def: The synagogue of Satan is the Lord's name in the Revelation for a body of religious persecutors who claimed the covenant name while opposing Christ and slandering His church. He speaks of it twice, to the two churches He does not rebuke. To Smyrna: "I know the blasphemy of them which say they are Jews, and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan" (Rev 2:9). To Philadelphia: "I will make them of the synagogue of Satan, which say they are Jews, and are not, but do lie; behold, I will make them to come and worship before thy feet, and to know that I have loved thee" (Rev 3:9). The phrase does not condemn a people by blood but exposes a false claim to covenant standing: those who boasted the outward name while rejecting the Messiah and harrying His followers had become, in truth, a gathering aligned with the accuser. It echoes the apostolic teaching that "he is not a Jew, which is one outwardly" but inwardly, by the circumcision of the heart (Rom 2:28-29), and that they are the true seed of Abraham who share Abraham's faith. The synagogue of Satan thus stands for all false, persecuting religion that wears the badge of God's people while serving His enemy — and over which the persevering church will at last be vindicated.
webster_summary: The Lord's name in Revelation 2:9 and 3:9 for false, persecuting religionists who claimed the covenant name while opposing Christ and slandering His church; over them the faithful church will be vindicated.

corruption_summary: The phrase is corrupted when it is wrenched into ethnic hatred against the Jewish people, the very error its context forbids, or when it is emptied so that no false, persecuting religion can ever be named.
corruption_paragraphs: Antisemitic abuse. The phrase has been wickedly seized to justify hatred of the Jewish people — a use that contradicts its own logic and the whole of Scripture. The text condemns not Jewish blood but a false claim to covenant standing joined to the persecution of Christ's church; the same apostle who recorded these words longed for his kinsmen's salvation (Rom 9:1-3; 10:1), and the gospel went "to the Jew first" (Rom 1:16). The dictionary repudiates every racial misuse of this verse and holds that the church owes the Jewish people the gospel, honor, and love, not contempt.

Reference-emptied misreading. The opposite error treats the phrase as too dangerous to mean anything, so that no counterfeit, persecuting religion may ever be exposed. But the Lord Himself named it, and named it to comfort a slandered church. The dictionary recovers the sober point: religion that wears God's badge while serving His enemy and harrying His people is, by Christ's own verdict, a synagogue of Satan — and the persevering church will be vindicated when its persecutors bow and learn that Christ has loved her.

etymology: From Revelation 2:17, the reward promised to the overcomer at Pergamos: "To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna." It recalls the pot of manna laid up before the LORD in the ark (Exo 16:33-34).
biblical_def: The hidden manna is the reward the glorified Christ promises to the overcomer at Pergamos: "To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written" (Rev 2:17). The image reaches back to the wilderness, where God fed Israel with manna, "bread from heaven," and commanded that a golden pot of it be laid up before the testimony in the ark as a memorial (Exo 16:32-34; Heb 9:4). That manna was hidden in the holiest place, unseen by the people. To the church at Pergamos — pressed to eat "things sacrificed unto idols" at the pagan feasts — Christ offers a better and secret food: Himself, the true bread from heaven (John 6:48-51). Those who refuse the idol's table are given to feed, hidden and unseen by the world, on the living Christ now, and to feast openly with Him in glory. The hidden manna is thus the soul's secret nourishment in communion with the Lord, the inner sustenance the world cannot see or share, kept for those who overcome the seductions of compromise. It is the answer of heaven to the believer who will not trade Christ for the brief satisfactions of idolatry.
webster_summary: The reward promised to the Pergamos overcomer in Revelation 2:17 — a secret, heavenly food recalling the manna laid up in the ark; Christ Himself, the true bread from heaven, the soul's hidden nourishment for those who refuse the idol's table.

corruption_summary: The hidden manna is corrupted when it is reduced to bare symbol with no living Christ to feed on, or when the secret communion it promises is replaced by a religion of mere outward experience and spectacle.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ-emptied symbolism. Treated as a poetic flourish, the hidden manna becomes a vague image of reward with no substance. Scripture fills it: the true bread from heaven is Christ Himself, given for the life of the world, on whom the soul feeds by faith (John 6). The dictionary holds that the promise is no empty figure but a pledge of real communion — the overcomer is nourished now and forever on the living Lord he refused to trade for idols.

Few entries face direct postmodern redefinition; here the danger is reductive. Where the hidden manna names a secret, inward feeding on Christ that the world cannot see, a spectacle-driven religion prizes only the visible and the sensational. The principle to recover is the hiddenness of true communion: the deepest nourishment of the saints is unseen by the world, kept in the holy place of fellowship with God, and tasted by those who overcome rather than by those who perform.

etymology: From Revelation 2:17, the token given to the overcomer at Pergamos: "a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it." White (Greek leukos) signifies purity, acquittal, and victory.
biblical_def: The white stone is the second part of the reward promised to the overcomer at Pergamos: "and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it" (Rev 2:17). In the ancient world a white stone served as a token of acquittal in a court (over against the black stone of condemnation), as a ticket of admission to a feast, and as a mark of welcome and favor. Each sense enriches the promise. To the overcomer Christ gives the verdict of acquittal, the admission to the marriage supper of the Lamb, and the personal token of His favor. Upon the stone is written "a new name" — known only to the one who receives it, a name expressing the intimate, particular love between the Lord and that soul, the new identity granted to those made new in Christ. As the Lord said to Israel, "thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the LORD shall name" (Isa 62:2). The white stone thus gathers up acquittal, welcome, and a love so personal that its name is a secret between the Savior and the saved. It is the pledge that the believer who overcomes the world's pressure to compromise is fully pardoned, fully welcomed, and fully and uniquely known by his Lord.
webster_summary: The token given to the Pergamos overcomer in Revelation 2:17, bearing a new name known only to its receiver; in the ancient world a sign of acquittal, admission, and favor — here Christ's pledge of pardon, welcome, and a uniquely personal love.

corruption_summary: The white stone is corrupted when its "new name" is taken for a charm of secret esoteric knowledge or self-invented identity, rather than the God-given name of pardon, welcome, and personal love granted in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Esoteric-charm misreading. Some treat the secret name as occult or gnostic knowledge, a hidden password earned by the initiated. The text says the opposite: the name is given by Christ to the one who overcomes by His grace, a token of acquittal and welcome, not a reward for esoteric attainment. The dictionary holds that the new name is the fruit of free pardon and personal love, written by the Lord, not decoded by the adept.

Self-made-identity misreading. A culture that prizes self-defined identity hears "new name" as a license to invent oneself. But in Scripture the new name is named by the mouth of the LORD (Isa 62:2); it is God's naming of the soul He has redeemed, expressing who the believer truly is in Christ. The dictionary recovers the order: identity is received from the Creator and Redeemer, not constructed by the creature. The white stone is Christ's word over us, sweeter and surer than any name we could give ourselves.
